```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                     fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.25)
```

A bird can go uncounted because it gives no cue or because the observer fails
to detect its cue. A combined distance and removal model separates these
processes while estimating abundance. First-detection time informs cue
availability. Distance informs perceptibility, the chance of detecting an
available bird. The model assumes that these processes are independent after
accounting for the modeled covariates.

This guide follows the combined model developed by Amundson et al. (2014) and
implemented in `unmarked::gdistremoval()`. Kellner et al. (2023) describe the
unmarked implementation and an application with point random effects. Here,
unmarked fits the full likelihood and multiScaleR optimizes environmental
neighborhoods around the survey points. Start with
`vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` for the spatial workflow.

The artificial data below demonstrate software behavior. They do not establish
scale recovery or interval coverage. The spatial optimization and full mapping
chunks are not run during vignette builds because they repeatedly fit the
hierarchical model. The native model and process predictions are evaluated.

# Separate the model components

The four formulas describe different parts of the model:

| Formula | Native prediction component | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `lambdaformula` | `"lambda"` | Latent abundance or density intensity |
| `phiformula` | `"phi"` | Additional availability between repeated visits |
| `removalformula` | `"rem"` | Cue probability during one unit of survey time |
| `distanceformula` | `"dist"` | Parameter of the distance detection key |

The `phi` component is estimated only with multiple primary periods. Its
availability describes temporary absence between visits, which differs from
cue availability during a survey. Primary periods do not automatically supply
a model of recruitment or survival. To model abundance changing among years,
define the appropriate site-year data and dependence structure first.

For a half-normal distance key, `"dist"` returns the detection standard
deviation in the input distance units. It is not a probability. This parameter
also differs from an environmental kernel width estimated by multiScaleR.
Environmental widths describe the neighborhood used to summarize habitat.

# Prepare spatial predictors and paired histories

Use different covariate names when the same raster source should have separate
scales in different processes. Reusing a covariate name shares its transform
and scale across all formulas that contain it.

```{r spatial-inputs}
set.seed(519)
habitat <- terra::rast(nrows = 30, ncols = 30, xmin = 0, xmax = 600,
  ymin = 0, ymax = 600, crs = "EPSG:26917")
xy <- terra::xyFromCell(habitat, seq_len(terra::ncell(habitat)))
terra::values(habitat) <- sin(xy[, 1] / 47) + cos(xy[, 2] / 61)
names(habitat) <- "habitat"
locations <- expand.grid(x = seq(110, 490, length.out = 6),
                         y = seq(110, 490, length.out = 6))
points <- sf::st_as_sf(locations, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 26917)
variables <- msr_vars(
  hab_abundance = kernel_var("habitat"),
  hab_presence = kernel_var("habitat"),
  hab_distance = kernel_var("habitat"),
  hab_removal = kernel_var("habitat"))
inputs <- kernel_prep(points, habitat, scale_vars = variables,
  kernel = "gaussian", sigma = rep(35, 4), max_D = 100,
  bin = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
site <- data.frame(site = seq_len(nrow(locations)), inputs$kernel_dat)
```

These four predictors initially summarize the same source at the same width.
The optimizer can subsequently change each width. Separate names allow this
choice; they do not guarantee that the data identify four useful scales.

Each detection supplies a distance class and a first-detection-time class.
For every site and visit, the two histories must have the same total. The
following simulation generates individuals once per site, then independently
samples their presence, cue time, and perceptibility on two visits.

```{r paired-data}
M <- nrow(site)
T <- 2L
distance_breaks <- c(0, 25, 60, 100)  # Meters from the observer
duration <- c(1, 2, 2)                # Five time units in three intervals
annual <- data.frame(date = rep(c(-0.5, 0.5), M))
time <- rep(seq(-0.5, 0.5, length.out = M * T), each = 3)
observation <- data.frame(time = time)
distance_counts <- removal_counts <- matrix(0, M, T * 3)
N <- rpois(M, exp(2 + 0.3 * site$hab_abundance))
for (i in seq_len(M)) for (visit in seq_len(T)) {
  row <- (i - 1L) * T + visit
  present <- rbinom(1, N[i], plogis(1 + 0.1 * site$hab_presence[i]))
  radius <- 100 * sqrt(runif(present))
  sigma <- exp(log(60) - 0.1 * site$hab_distance[i] + 0.2 * annual$date[row])
  perceived <- runif(present) < exp(-radius^2 / (2 * sigma^2))
  cue <- plogis(-0.5 + 0.1 * site$hab_removal[i] + 0.2 * time[(row - 1L) * 3 + 1L])
  first_time <- rgeom(present, cue) + 1L
  detected <- perceived & first_time <= sum(duration)
  cols <- (visit - 1L) * 3 + seq_len(3)
  distance_counts[i, cols] <- tabulate(cut(radius[detected], distance_breaks,
    labels = FALSE), nbins = 3)
  removal_counts[i, cols] <- tabulate(cut(first_time[detected], c(0, cumsum(duration)),
    labels = FALSE), nbins = 3)
}
frame <- unmarked::unmarkedFrameGDR(distance_counts, removal_counts,
  numPrimary = T, siteCovs = site, yearlySiteCovs = annual,
  obsCovs = observation, dist.breaks = distance_breaks,
  unitsIn = "m", period.lengths = duration)
```

Site covariates have `M` rows. Yearly or visit covariates have `M * T` rows,
ordered by site and then visit. Observation covariates have `M * T * 3` rows,
ordered by site, visit, and removal interval. These orders must remain paired
with the response matrices. Retain site keys so that spatial preparations can
be joined without rearranging detection histories.

Optimized raster predictors currently enter `siteCovs`. Ordinary visit and
observation covariates remain in their original slots. Avoid putting the same
optimized name in those slots, where it would shadow the updated site value.
Changing raster values within a primary-period series or estimating
year-varying widths requires an additional supported model specification.

# Fit the joint model and optimize scales

```{r native-fit}
base_model <- unmarked::gdistremoval(
  lambdaformula = ~hab_abundance,
  phiformula = ~hab_presence,
  removalformula = ~hab_removal + time,
  distanceformula = ~hab_distance + date,
  data = frame, mixture = "P", keyfun = "halfnorm",
  output = "density", unitsOut = "ha", K = 40, se = FALSE)
```

The native model here omits coefficient SEs to keep the build short. Obtain
native uncertainty for a real analysis and check convergence and sensitivity
to `K`, the upper bound used to sum over latent abundance. A larger `K` should
not materially change estimates or predictions once the sum is adequate.

```{r scale-fit, eval=FALSE}
base_model <- unmarked::update(base_model, se = TRUE)
# Skip intermediate coefficient Hessians, but retain them for returned fits.
fit <- multiScale_optim(base_model, inputs, join_by = site["site"],
  par = rep(35 / inputs$unit_conv, 4), refit_fn = refit_gdistremoval,
  backend = "refit", verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit)
plot_marginal_effects(fit, type = "lambda", ylab = "Density intensity per ha")
plot_marginal_effects(fit, type = "dist", ylab = "Distance key parameter (m)")
plot_marginal_effects(fit, type = "rem", ylab = "Cue probability per time unit")
```

The optional `refit_gdistremoval()` callback skips coefficient Hessians during
scalar objective evaluations. It retains the original model's `se` setting
for returned fits, including the final selected model. It preserves the native
likelihood, optimizer controls, and coefficient starts. The default refit policy
is unchanged. The callback can also be passed to PSOCK workers without copying
local data into a closure.

Read each scale estimate as the neighborhood width for its named covariate.
A broad interval or a width near the search extent calls for inspection of
the likelihood profile and alternative starts. The component effect plots
hold other covariates at reference values and set group deviations to zero.
They describe component parameters, not the combined observation process.

Supported random intercepts and slopes remain native unmarked model terms.
Adding `(1 | route)` to a supported formula selects its TMB fitting engine.
At unsampled groups, an explicit `re.form = NA` sets group deviations to zero.
It does not average over the distribution of random effects.

# Read the complete observation process

```{r process-predictions}
process <- predict_gdistremoval(base_model)
head(process[, c("site", "period", "density", "phi", "availability",
                 "perceptibility", "detection", "expected_count")])
```

How to read this output:

| Output | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| `density` | Detection-adjusted mean individuals per fitted area unit |
| `phi` | Availability between visits; one if the fitted model has one visit |
| `availability` | Chance of giving a cue during the complete survey |
| `perceptibility` | Distance-integrated chance of detecting an available cue |
| `detection` | Product of the three observation-process probabilities |
| `expected_count` | Mean number the specified survey would record |

Density and expected count answer different questions. A site can have high
density and a low expected count when cue availability or perceptibility is
low. The helper uses each visit's distance parameter and applies unequal
removal durations before combining intervals. These are point estimates.
Their attributes identify the area units, survey area, and conditioning.

For large prediction grids, half-normal and exponential keys use vectorized
closed integrals, with repeated distance scales evaluated once. The hazard
key uses numerical integration. These calculations retain the native distance
units and the point-transect area measure.

When `phi` is modeled, latent abundance and density describe the site's
superpopulation. Multiplying either by `phi` gives its mean available during
that visit, before cue availability and perceptibility. Choose the population
quantity before interpreting or adding up predictions across a state.

With `mixture = "ZIP"`, native `"lambda"` is the Poisson-component intensity.
`predict_gdistremoval()` multiplies that intensity by the nonstructural-zero
probability when calculating abundance, density, and expected counts. It
uses the fitted zero-inflation parameter on its logit scale. NB uses the native
negative-binomial mean without this ZIP adjustment.

# Predict at new grid sites

For a native lambda map, prepare rasters with the fitted transformations and
training normalization. Keep source coverage beyond the state boundary so
that neighborhoods at its edge have the intended support. Crop the final
prediction afterward. A density map needs only the covariates in its state
formula; detection-only date, time, or observer values do not need to be
invented for it.

```{r native-map, eval=FALSE}
transformed <- kernel_scale.raster(habitat, multiScaleR = fit,
  scale_vars = variables[variables$covariate == "hab_abundance", , drop = FALSE],
  scale_center = TRUE, match_buffer = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
density_intensity <- predict(fit, transformed, type = "lambda")
terra::plot(density_intensity)
```

Only the state predictor needs projection for this map. Other component maps
require their own spatial layers and explicit date, time, or observer scenarios
when used by the formula.

To obtain unconditional ZIP means or compare complete survey scenarios on an
even grid, construct an explicit prediction frame. Zero histories specify the
row layout, not observations to refit. The following example uses a small
subset of raster-cell centers; extend it in batches for a large state grid.

```{r grid-process, eval=FALSE}
cells <- c(225, 236, 405, 416)
grid_xy <- terra::xyFromCell(habitat, cells)
grid <- sf::st_as_sf(data.frame(grid_xy), coords = c("x", "y"),
                     crs = terra::crs(habitat))
grid_inputs <- kernel_prep(grid, habitat, scale_vars = variables,
  max_D = fit$max_D, kernel = "gaussian", bin = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
keys <- data.frame(site = seq_len(nrow(grid_xy)))
zeros <- matrix(0, nrow(grid_xy), T * 3)
grid_frame <- unmarked::unmarkedFrameGDR(zeros, zeros,
  numPrimary = T, siteCovs = keys,
  yearlySiteCovs = data.frame(date = rep(c(-0.5, 0.5), nrow(grid_xy))),
  obsCovs = data.frame(time = rep(0, nrow(grid_xy) * T * 3)),
  dist.breaks = distance_breaks, unitsIn = "m", period.lengths = duration)
grid_prediction <- predict_gdistremoval(fit, grid_frame, grid_inputs,
  join_by = keys, re.form = NA)
grid_prediction[, c("site", "period", "density", "expected_count")]
```

The helper joins fitted spatial covariates into the frame using explicit keys.
It leaves nonspatial scenario values unchanged and does not standardize the
new prediction sample again. For density totals, multiply density by actual
nonoverlapping cell areas, including boundary fractions. Summing counts from
overlapping survey circles would double-count their spatial support.

# Simulate conditional checks and validate geographic prediction

```{r conditional-simulation}
set.seed(724)
replicates <- simulate_gdistremoval(base_model, nsim = 2)
# Each visit's distance and removal histories describe the same detections.
first_distance_total <- rowSums(replicates[[1]]@yDistance[, 1:3])
first_removal_total <- rowSums(replicates[[1]]@yRemoval[, 1:3])
all(first_distance_total == first_removal_total)
```

The simulator draws latent abundance once per site and shares it across visits.
It then draws visit counts and allocates them to distance and removal classes.
It supports P, NB, and ZIP mixtures, including uniform distance keys, and keeps
incomplete survey histories missing. It uses the integrated calculations in
this guide rather than changing unmarked's installed methods.

These simulations condition on fitted coefficients, spatial widths, and the
chosen random-effect policy. They do not draw new group effects or quantify
uncertainty in estimated variances. A bootstrap intended to include scale or
model selection must repeat those fitting steps and respect the sampling
design. The current Bayesian multiScaleR interface does not implement this
imperfect-detection likelihood.

Before transferring a model statewide, check detection fit, distance/time
independence, sensitivity to distance truncation, covariate support, and
geographic coverage. Validate with spatial blocks that keep repeated records
from a site together. Estimate scales and select models within each training
fold so that held-out outcomes cannot influence those choices. A successful
map operation does not establish predictive performance in unsampled regions.

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval=FALSE}
# 1. Fit the complete native model, with its original observation structure.
native <- unmarked::gdistremoval(~hab_abundance, ~hab_presence,
  ~hab_removal + time, ~hab_distance + date, data = frame,
  output = "density", K = 40)
# 2. Estimate named environmental scales without replacing the likelihood.
fit <- multiScale_optim(native, inputs, join_by = site["site"],
  backend = "refit", refit_fn = refit_gdistremoval)
# 3. Inspect native component effects and complete survey expectations.
plot_marginal_effects(fit, type = "rem")
survey <- predict_gdistremoval(fit)
# 4. Simulate conditional paired histories for model checks.
replicate <- simulate_gdistremoval(fit)[[1]]
# 5. Apply fitted transforms at new sites; retain training normalization.
future <- predict_gdistremoval(fit, grid_frame, grid_inputs, join_by = keys)
```

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `multiScale_optim()` | Optimize spatial covariates through native joint-model refits |
| `refit_gdistremoval()` | Skip objective Hessians while retaining final native uncertainty settings |
| `prepare_unmarked_data()` | Prepare explicit native component-prediction rows |
| `predict_gdistremoval()` | Combine state and observation components into interpretable means |
| `simulate_gdistremoval()` | Draw conditional paired histories with matched survey totals |
| `plot_marginal_effects()` | Inspect active state, availability, distance, or removal effects |

See also:

- `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` for spatial preparation.
- `vignette("feature-compatibility", package = "multiScaleR")` for fitting and prediction boundaries.
- `vignette("spatial_projection_clamping", package = "multiScaleR")` for projection and extrapolation choices.

combining distance sampling and time removal to estimate detection probability
during avian point counts. *The Auk* 131:476-494.

Kellner, K. F., Smith, A. D., Royle, J. A., Kéry, M., Belant, J. L., and
